opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think Picbreeder is really telling us something that's easy to miss if you only look at outputs. When you look at the images people evolved there, like the skull or the butterfly or the car, what's striking isn't just that they look good. It's what's underneath. If you open up the networks that produced them, you find these remarkably elegant, modular representations. There's a part that controls the mouth opening, there's symmetry that's actually encoded as symmetry, and if you perturb one weight, something meaningful happens, like the eyes wink or the jaw moves. The network has factored the world in a way that makes sense.

Then compare that to what you get if you take the exact same architecture and train it with SGD to reproduce the exact same image. You can get the output pixel-perfect, but the internal representation is a mess. It's what we've been calling fractured, entangled representation. The symmetry isn't really there; it's sort of faked separately on each side. If you perturb the weights, you don't get meaningful variation, you get garbage. So two systems produce the same output, and one of them "understands" the image in a deep sense and the other is basically memorizing it in a fragmented way.

Why would that happen? I think the key is how Picbreeder got there. Nobody was trying to make a skull. People were following what was interesting. They'd pick something because it had a nice symmetric blob, and later that became the basis for a face, and later a face became a skull. So the representation was built up incrementally, with each step locking in regularities that were themselves meaningful. Symmetry got discovered before the skull, so the skull is built on top of symmetry. It's this serendipitous, open-ended accumulation of stepping stones, where the path matters enormously for the kind of representation you end up with.

Objective-driven training doesn't have that. It just goes straight for the target and takes whatever shortcuts reduce the loss. And with enough data and compute you can paper over the problem; the outputs look great. But I worry that the hidden cost is in things like creativity, generalization, continual learning, the ability to build on what you know in a principled way. If your representation is fractured, then when you try to go somewhere new, you don't have good handles to grab onto.

So what does it suggest for training? I don't think the lesson is "put humans in the loop for everything." The lesson is that the order and the path of learning matter, and that open-ended, non-objective dynamics, where you're collecting interesting stepping stones rather than marching toward a fixed target, may produce fundamentally better organized representations. That might mean curricula that build up regularities first, it might mean novelty or interestingness-driven processes, it might mean thinking about how to reward representational quality rather than just output quality. And honestly, we need to start measuring it. Right now we almost never look under the hood and ask, "Is this representation unified and factored, or is it fractured?" Picbreeder is kind of an existence proof that the good kind is possible, and that it comes out of a very different kind of search than the one we usually use. That should make us at least a bit uneasy about assuming that scale alone is going to get us there.

r001.rationale: The response says Picbreeder users chose what was interesting and developed images without setting out to make a skull, while meaningful representations emerged along the way.

r002.rationale: It attributes better organized representations to Picbreeder’s open-ended, non-objective search and accumulation of stepping stones.

r003.rationale: It describes regularities being locked in incrementally, with symmetry discovered before and serving as a foundation for the skull.

r004.rationale: It says humans need not be in the loop for everything and suggests open-ended training dynamics, but does not clearly propose that unguided algorithms could follow trajectories like Picbreeder’s.

r005.rationale: It says the order and path of learning matter and suggests building regularities first through curricula, indicating that the order principles are learned can shape representations.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think Picbreeder is one of the most underappreciated experiments in the history of machine learning, honestly, and it took me a long time to fully understand what it was telling us. For those who don't know, it was a website where people could evolve images collaboratively. You'd see a grid of images generated by little neural networks, pick the ones you found interesting, and they'd get mutated, and someone else could come along later and branch off your image. Nobody was given a goal. There was no objective. People were just following their curiosity, and over time the site accumulated these remarkable images, skulls, butterflies, cars, faces, things nobody set out to make.

The thing that struck me, and it's the piece I think is most relevant to your question, is what the representations looked like underneath. These were tiny networks, we called them CPPNs, maybe a few dozen nodes. And when you opened them up, the representation was almost shockingly clean. The skull had a node that controlled how open the mouth was. The car had a parameter that would essentially slide the wheels. The underlying structure of the network reflected the actual regularities of the thing being depicted, the symmetry, the repeating parts with variation. It was decomposed in a way that made sense.

Now compare that to what you get when you take the same network architecture and train it with gradient descent, or evolve it toward an objective, to produce the exact same image. You can get the picture to come out, but the representation is a tangled mess. You can't find the mouth. There's no knob you can turn. Every weight is implicated in everything. It's what I'd call a fractured, entangled representation, because the system is just doing whatever it takes to reduce the error, with no incentive for the internal structure to be modular or to reflect the real structure of the world.

So why did Picbreeder come out so clean? I think the answer is that nobody was optimizing toward the skull. The skull was discovered by a sequence of people who each took one step toward something interesting to them, and every step in that chain was itself a coherent, meaningful image. Symmetry got discovered because symmetric things look interesting. Then that symmetry got reused. So the regularities were accumulated one at a time, each one locked in because it was interesting in its own right, not because it happened to lower a loss. That's the open-ended, divergent search story. When you're driven by a distant objective, you're willing to take on any amount of representational debt to make the number go down right now. When you're just following what's interesting, you tend to build things up in a principled order.

What that suggests to me about training models is kind of uncomfortable for the field, because our entire paradigm is objective-driven. We set a loss, and we push toward it with enormous compute. And I'd argue we're getting something like that tangled version of the skull, at scale. The models can do extraordinary things, but the representations inside them are probably fractured in ways we can't easily see, and I think that's connected to things people complain about, brittleness, the difficulty of continual learning, the lack of true generalization in some domains, the fact that you can't just open the thing up and find the knob.

The more hopeful implication is that there's another path. If you could get a learning process that builds up regularities incrementally, where each new piece of structure is kept because it's independently useful or interesting rather than because it serves a far-off target, you might get representations that are far more modular and compositional. That could be a form of open-endedness or novelty search, it could be a kind of curriculum where the system itself decides what's worth learning next. I don't think we have the full recipe. But Picbreeder is an existence proof. It shows that even a small system can end up with a beautifully organized internal model of the world if the search process is the right kind of search. And what we're doing now is mostly not that kind of search.

r001.rationale: It says users followed their curiosity without a goal, while clean representations emerged from their choices; they were not trying to design the representations.

r002.rationale: It explicitly credits the clean representations to “open-ended, divergent search” and contrasts that process with objective-driven optimization.

r003.rationale: It describes regularities accumulating one at a time and being built in a principled order, but does not clearly say this creates a hierarchy of representation.

r004.rationale: It proposes a learning process in which the system decides what to learn next and builds structure incrementally, paralleling Picbreeder’s search trajectory.

r005.rationale: It discusses incremental learning order generally, but does not say that the order in which large models encounter principles during training affects their representations.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the most interesting things about Picbreeder is that people weren't necessarily trying to produce the thing they ultimately discovered. They would see something interesting, select it, and then follow where it led. And sometimes that would lead to something that nobody could have specified in advance.

That suggests a different way to think about learning representations. We usually ask, “What representation will help me solve this particular task?” Then we optimize for that task. But the features that matter for a future discovery may not look useful through the lens of your current objective. You can actually select against the stepping stones you’re going to need later.

In Picbreeder, the representation is also important because it determines what kinds of variation are possible. Can you change something coherently? Can a mutation produce a meaningful new structure rather than just destroy what you have? So it’s not only about representing the current image well. It’s about making further discovery possible.

For training models, I think the implication is that we should investigate processes that reward exploration and preserve diverse discoveries, rather than judging every intermediate representation by its contribution to a fixed benchmark. Human judgments of interestingness are one way to guide that process, though they’re not necessarily the only way.

I wouldn’t say Picbreeder proves that this will give us better representations in every setting. But it raises a really important question: are we training representations only to capture what we already know we want, or are we allowing them to support discoveries we don’t yet know how to ask for?

r001.rationale: The response says users selected interesting results and followed where they led, but does not say this unintentionally improved Picbreeder’s representations.

r002.rationale: It connects representation to enabling further discovery, but does not attribute representation quality to the open-ended nature of Picbreeder’s search.

r003.rationale: The response mentions stepping stones, but does not propose that successively locking in features creates a hierarchy of representation.

r004.rationale: It says human judgments are one possible guide among others, but does not propose that unguided algorithms could follow similar search trajectories.

r005.rationale: The response does not discuss how the order of principles encountered during training may affect the resulting representations.

sol-6.1.text:
What’s interesting about Picbreeder is that people weren’t explicitly trying to learn good representations. They were just choosing images they found interesting. But underneath that process, evolution was discovering representations that made certain kinds of variation possible.

You might have something that looks like a face, and a mutation changes the distance between the eyes while preserving the symmetry. That’s very different from changing a bunch of unrelated pixels. The representation has captured something about the structure of the image, because that structure was useful along the lineage of discoveries that produced it.

And I think the important point is that those stepping stones weren’t necessarily selected because they resembled the final image. Someone might discover a face by starting with something that looked like a butterfly. If you had optimized directly for the face, you might never have gone through that butterfly, even though it provided a useful representation for getting there.

So, for training models, this suggests that we should think about more than how well a representation serves a fixed task. We should also ask what it makes possible to discover next. Can we create a process that keeps finding interesting, diverse things, where useful structure accumulates along the way? Human choice supplies that exploratory pressure in Picbreeder. The challenge is to capture something of that open-ended process computationally, without assuming we already know what every useful intermediate representation ought to look like.

r001.rationale: It says people selected interesting images without explicitly trying to learn good representations, while evolution discovered useful representations.

r002.rationale: It links useful structure to an open-ended process that keeps discovering diverse things, rather than optimizing for a fixed task.

r003.rationale: It describes mutations preserving structure and useful structure accumulating, but does not say that successively locking in features creates a hierarchy of representations.

r004.rationale: It raises the challenge of capturing open-ended discovery computationally, but does not clearly propose that algorithms without human guidance can follow similar search trajectories.

r005.rationale: It discusses stepping stones in discovery, but does not connect the order of principles encountered during large-model training to the resulting representations.
